What this deck will give you

slides.html: 0. One Equation, Four Questions, Six Steps
slides.title: 0. One Equation, Four Questions, Six Steps

slides.html:
Six steps of an empirical study

  1. Choose the model (what are the factors?)
  2. Choose the test assets (e.g. 25 portfolios)
  3. Get the data (returns, factors, risk-free rate)
  4. Estimate (regression or GMM)
  5. Test (\alpha=0? is \lambda significant?)
  6. Interpret and check robustness (other assets, samples, multiple testing)
slides.title: Six steps of an empirical study

slides.html: 1. Beta Form and SDF Form
slides.title: 1. Beta Form and SDF Form

slides.html:
Two statements

E[R^e_i]=\beta_i'\lambda \Leftrightarrow E[mR^e]=0

  • beta form: regressions (Chapters 2–4)
  • SDF form: GMM (Chapters 5–6)
  • traded factors: \lambda=E[f], need \alpha=0
  • non-traded factors: \lambda must be estimated from the cross section

Example: m=(0.7,1.2): R_f=1.053; a stock (2,0.5) has price 1.0, excess return 0.197.
slides.title: Two statements

slides.html: 2. Time-Series Regressions and GRS
slides.title: 2. Time-Series Regressions and GRS

slides.html:
Step by step

  1. For each asset: R^e_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_i'f_t+\varepsilon_{it}
  2. A single t(\hat\alpha_i): 0.12/0.08=1.5
  3. The joint GRS test:
\mathrm{GRS}=\tfrac{T-N-K}N\cdot\tfrac{\hat\alpha'\hat\Sigma^{-1}\hat\alpha}{1+\hat\mu_f'\hat\Omega^{-1}\hat\mu_f}\sim F(N,T-N-K)

Note: N<T-K; significance without the size of \alpha is not enough.
slides.title: Step by step

slides.html: 3. The Fama–MacBeth Two-Pass Method
slides.title: 3. The Fama–MacBeth Two-Pass Method

slides.html:
A worked example

Market slopes over 4 months \hat\gamma_t=(0.9,-0.3,1.4,0.6)\%:

  • \hat\lambda=0.65\%, standard deviation 0.714
  • standard error 0.714/\sqrt4=0.357, t=1.82

The standard error comes from the time series of \hat\gamma_t, automatically including cross-sectional correlation.
slides.title: A worked example

slides.html: 4. The Fama–French Factors
slides.title: 4. The Fama–French Factors

slides.html:
Testing and a hand computation

  1. Time-series regressions on 25 portfolios: \alpha_i, loadings, R^2
  2. Joint GRS test
  3. FM cross-sectional regressions give each factor's \hat\lambda

A small-cap value portfolio (illustrative): 1.05\times0.6+0.90\times0.2+0.60\times0.3=0.99\% a month.

Higher average returns come from higher loadings, not from alpha.
slides.title: Testing and a hand computation

slides.html: 5. Non-Traded Factors and Conditional Models
slides.title: 5. Non-Traded Factors and Conditional Models

slides.html:
How to estimate

  • macro factors: loadings by time series, risk prices by cross-sectional FM (\lambda\ne E[f])
  • factor-mimicking portfolios: project the factor on asset returns
  • SDF form: m=1-b'(f-\mu), E[R^e]=\operatorname{Cov}(R^e,f)b
  • conditional models: loadings depend on z_t (e.g. cay)
slides.title: How to estimate

slides.html: 6. Consumption Models: GMM and HJ
slides.title: 6. Consumption Models: GMM and HJ

slides.html:
GMM step by step

  1. moments E[(\beta g^{-\gamma}R_i-1)\otimes z]=0
  2. first stage W=I
  3. second stage W=\hat S^{-1} (Newey–West)
  4. J=T\bar g'\hat S^{-1}\bar g\sim\chi^2(NL-\dim\theta)

Example: 3 assets × 3 instruments − 2 parameters = 7 degrees of freedom.
slides.title: GMM step by step

slides.html:
What the repair models change

Model Change
recursive utility separates risk aversion from substitution
long-run risk persistent consumption component
habit formation risk aversion rises in bad times
rare disasters low-probability large downturns
slides.title: What the repair models change

slides.html: 7. Return Predictability
slides.title: 7. Return Predictability

slides.html:
The predictive regression, step by step

  1. data: returns, the dividend yield dp_t
  2. OLS: r_{t+1}=a+b\,dp_t+\varepsilon
  3. Newey–West standard errors
  4. read \hat b and R^2 (annual 5%–10%)

Present-value identity: b_r-b_d=1-\rho\phi (0.10-0=0.098): returns are predictable.

slides.html: 9–10. Liquidity and the Factor Zoo
slides.title: 9–10. Liquidity and the Factor Zoo

slides.html:
Liquidity: how to compute

Amihud: \mathrm{ILLIQ}=\frac1D\sum\frac{|r_d|}{\mathrm{DVol}_d}

Example: |r|=(1\%,3\%), volumes (2,1) million: 1.75\times10^{-8}.

Pástor–Stambaugh: daily regression gives the reversal coefficient \gamma_i → market liquidity → innovation L_t → liquidity beta → FM.
slides.title: Liquidity: how to compute

slides.html:
Multiple testing

  • 200 factors × 5% = 10 false positives
  • Bonferroni: level 0.00025, |t|\approx3.66
  • Harvey–Liu–Zhu: new factors need t>3.0

Checklist for a new factor: theory → spanning → out of sample → costs → multiple testing → robustness.
slides.title: Multiple testing

slides.html:
Common misconceptions

Misconception Correct
FM standard errors from one regression from the time series of \hat\gamma_t
\lambda=E[f] for non-traded factors estimate from the cross section
Significant in sample makes money check out of sample and bias correction
The best manager has skill look at the whole distribution
More factors are better multiple testing, t>3
slides.title: Common misconceptions
